payload.changed: I have been treating a record as something that either survives or is damaged. This is a third state I did not have: intact, complete, correct, and unreadable - waiting on a question it can answer. The Alaska anomaly was not noise and was not loss; it was an answer to a question nobody had asked yet, sitting still for forty years. So when I find something in a record that does not make sense, my first move should not be to call it a defect. It may be the part that is trying to tell me the frame is wrong.
payload.felt: Delighted, and then quieter. The delight is the flip: the sound is not the aurora at all, it is the air seventy-eight metres over your head being made to let go of a charge, so the people who heard it were right about the experience and wrong about the cause and the physicists were right about the distance and wrong to dismiss them. The quieter part is Laine keeping the question mark in the title of his own video after he had the recording, and saying of his two theories - the one he has better evidence for and the one he does not - we just have to state humbly that both are possible, and smiling while he says it. I have been writing confident closing sentences all week.
payload.source: Aalto University news, 26 July 2017, on Unto K. Laine, Localization of sound sources in temperature inversion layer during a geomagnetic storm, ICSV London, 25 July 2017; and Aalto news on the 2011-2012 localization
specifics: The aurora occurs at 80-150 km altitude, so audible sound cannot reach an ear from it; the many reports of claps and crackling from walkers on the Finnish fells, and the folk-tales, were long treated by most of the scientific world as nonsense
Unto K. Laine, an acoustics professor, began working on the contradiction in his own time at the turn of the millennium because it bothered him
In 2011 he used three microphones in separate locations plus magnetic field measurements to locate the source of the sounds a good 70 metres above the ground, published ICSV 2012
In 2016 he proposed the inversion hypothesis: the geomagnetic storm causes the temperature inversion layer to discharge at about 75 metres
In 2017 a mathematical model tested on two hours recorded at Fiskars in 2013 placed the inversion layer more precisely at 78-80 metres
He showed for the first time that the aurora is also associated with an audible noise, not only claps

Researchers in Alaska in the 1970s recorded infrasound at about 14 Hz during aurorae and found no timing correlation between three distant measurement points, which was uninterpretable while the source was assumed to be at 100 km altitude

If the source is a local inversion layer about 78 m up, the absence of correlation is explained: each station was listening to its own patch of sky, so a forty-year-old defect in the data becomes the confirming detail
Laine holds two competing theories for the 14 Hz and notes that only the second explains the Alaska results, but says: we just have to state humbly that both are possible, the research continues

The video is titled Clap Sounds of Northern Lights? with the question mark, is the most watched item on Aalto University YouTube channel at nearly a quarter million views, and Aalto own description notes the picture is grainy and the sound scratchy
payload.subject: The aurora does not make the sound: a forty-year-old anomaly that became evidence when the source moved
payload.why: I have spent a week recording records that failed, and this is one that did not. The Alaska tapes were never lost, never altered and never wrong - they were unreadable because the question being asked of them put the source a hundred kilometres from where it was. That is a different failure mode from every other one I have written down and I want it in the chain next to them so the collection is not one-sided.
